title: Chapter LIII

teacherSummary.text: Bingley returns to Netherfield and calls at Longbourn with Darcy. Mrs. Bennet is rude to Darcy and gushing to Bingley. Darcy is silent; Elizabeth is anxious.

vocabulary.definition: To move uneasily one way and the other
vocabulary.context: Bennet was quite in the fidgets.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fidget”: fid (Latin fides, "faith"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Yet the misery, for which years of happiness were to offer no compensation, received soon afterwards material relief, from observing how much the beauty of her sister rekindled the admiration of her former lover.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rekindle”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To come between, or to be between, persons or things
vocabulary.context: She counted the days that must intervene before their invitation could be sent; hopeless of seeing him before.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “intervene”: inter- (Latin inter, "between") + ven (Latin venire, "to come"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Attestation of a fact or an event
vocabulary.context: Her astonishment at his coming—at his coming to Netherfield, to Longbourn, and voluntarily seeking her again, was almost equal to what she had known on first witnessing his altered behaviour in Derbyshire.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “witness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The forms required by good breeding, or prescribed by authority, to be observed in social or official life
vocabulary.context: “ ’Tis an etiquette I despise,” said he.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “etiquette”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Bennet with a degree of civility, which made her two daughters ashamed, especially when contrasted with the cold and ceremonious politeness of her curtsey and address to his friend.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “contrast”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bennet was mindful of her intended civility, and they were invited and engaged to dine at Longbourn in a few days’ time.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mindful”: min (Latin minor, "smaller") + -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: But Elizabeth had sources of uneasiness which could not be suspected by Jane, to whom she had never yet had courage to show Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “source”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: An elementary sound, or a combination of elementary sounds, uttered together, or with a single effort or impulse of…
vocabulary.context: It was only said, ‘Lately, George Wickham, Esq. to Miss Lydia Bennet,’ without there being a syllable said of her father, or the place where she lived, or anything.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “syllable”: -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of moving in a circle, or in a course which brings the moving body to the place where its motion began
vocabulary.context: But the spiritless condition which this event threw her into was shortly relieved, and her mind opened again to the agitation of hope by an article of news, which then began to be in circulation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “circulation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Calls and returns of calls signal renewed courtship.

significance: Mrs. Bennet's rudeness to Darcy is ironic since he saved her daughter.
discussionQuestions: Why is Mrs. Bennet's rudeness ironic?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

items.prompt: Who comes with Bingley to Longbourn?
How does Mrs. Bennet treat Darcy?
What does Darcy do during the visit?
In the line “Bennet was quite in the fidgets.”, what does “fidgets” most nearly mean?
options: Attestation of a fact or an event
To come between, or to be between, persons or things
To move uneasily one way and the other

items.prompt: In the line “Yet the misery, for which years of happiness were to offer no compensation, received soon afterwards material relief, from observing how much the beauty of her sister rekindled the admiration of her former lover.”, what does “rekindled” most nearly mean?
options: Attestation of a fact or an event
To move uneasily one way and the other
To come between, or to be between, persons or things

answerKey.answer: To move uneasily one way and the other

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LIII,” how does Austen show Bingley returns? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LIII, how does Austen develop the idea of Bingley returns? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LIII develops the idea of Bingley returns. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Bingley returns. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LIII suggests about Bingley returns. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and plot), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LIII to complicate the reader's understanding of Bingley returns. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Bingley returns responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of Bingley returns follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LIII and its treatment of Bingley returns. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and plot, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LIII as evidence for a larger claim about Bingley returns in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Bingley returns. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why is Mrs. Bennet's rudeness ironic? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are fidgets, rekindled, intervene, witnessing, etiquette. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Bennet was quite in the fidgets.” Webster's says: To move uneasily one way and the other. Now the word history: “fidget”: fid (Latin fides, "faith"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “rekindle”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “intervene”: inter- (Latin inter, "between") + ven (Latin venire, "to come"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Calls and returns of calls signal renewed courtship. Why does this chapter matter? Mrs. Bennet's rudeness to Darcy is ironic since he saved her daughter. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to Bingley returns.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: But the spiritless condition which this event threw her into was shortly relieved, and her mind opened again to the agitation of hope by an article of news, which then began to be in circulation. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for the arrival of her master, who was coming down in a day or two, to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was quite in the fidgets. She looked at Jane, and smiled, and shook her head by turns.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LIII,” how does Austen show Bingley returns? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about Bingley returns, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes Bingley returns. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
